chapter.name: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
chapter.blurb: How the matter around us is classified into mixtures, pure substances, elements and compounds: mixtures as combinations of substances that each keep their own properties, classified as uniform or non-uniform depending on whether their components can be told apart; pure substances as consisting of only one type of particle; elements as substances made of identical atoms that cannot be broken down further, shown by passing electric current through water to yield hydrogen and oxygen; compounds as entirely new substances formed when elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio, shown by heating sugar and by heating iron with sulfur to form iron sulfide; how elements, compounds and mixtures are put to use in daily life and technology; and minerals as natural substances that are usually compounds but occasionally pure native elements.

scope_in.item: Mixtures: two or more substances mixed together, each retaining its own properties, with components that do not react chemically with each other
Non-uniform mixtures, where components are visible with the naked eye or a magnifying device (poha; sprout salad of green gram, chickpeas, onion and tomato)
Uniform mixtures, where components cannot be distinguished even under a microscope (sugar dissolved in water)
Air as a uniform mixture of nitrogen (about 78 percent, does not take part in combustion), oxygen (needed for life and combustion), argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour

Activity 8.1: lime water (calcium hydroxide solution) turns milky when left exposed to air, confirming carbon dioxide in air; word equation Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide gives Calcium carbonate + Water
Activity 8.2: a black sheet of paper left undisturbed near an open window collects tiny dust particles, showing dust is suspended in air and is considered a pollutant, not an integral part of the air
Alloys as uniform mixtures of metals: stainless steel (iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon), brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin)
Pure substances: in science, a substance with no other substance present in it, consisting of the same type of particles, that cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by any physical process

The everyday meaning of 'pure' (unadulterated) versus the scientific meaning; adulteration as illegally adding cheaper or poor-quality substances to increase quantity or reduce manufacturing cost, which can make a product hazardous to health

Activity 8.3: passing electric current through acidified water using a 9 V battery produces gas at each terminal; a pop sound with a burning candle identifies hydrogen, a brighter glowing flame identifies oxygen; word equation Water gives Hydrogen + Oxygen

Elements: pure substances made up of identical particles called atoms, which cannot be broken down into simpler substances and are the building blocks of matter; examples hydrogen, oxygen, gold, silver, sulfur and carbon
Atoms of most elements combine to form molecules (two atoms of hydrogen combine to form one molecule of hydrogen; two atoms of oxygen combine to form one molecule of oxygen)

Compounds: formed when different elements combine in a fixed ratio to form something entirely new, with properties different from the constituent elements, and which cannot be separated by physical methods; water (hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 atom ratio) and sodium chloride (sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio) as examples

Activity 8.4: heating sugar in a boiling tube produces water droplets and finally chars to leave behind carbon, showing sugar decomposes into carbon, hydrogen and oxygen and so is a compound, not an element

Activity 8.5, Sample A (iron filings and sulfur powder mixed, unheated): a mixture, with black and yellow particles visible, attracted by a magnet, reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid to give iron chloride and a colourless, odourless gas (hydrogen) that pops with a flame

Activity 8.5, Sample B (iron and sulfur heated together, then ground): the compound iron sulfide, a uniform black mass not attracted by a magnet, reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid to give iron chloride and hydrogen sulfide gas with a rotten-egg odour

Uses of elements, compounds and mixtures: air (mixture) and water (compound) essential for life; iron and aluminium (elements) used to construct bridges, buildings and vehicles; chemists combine elements to make medicines, vaccines and fertilisers; engineers use compounds and mixtures such as stainless steel, wood, steel and concrete for their unique properties

Minerals: most rocks are a mixture of minerals; native minerals are pure elements such as gold, silver, copper, sulfur and carbon; most minerals are compounds such as quartz, calcite, mica, pyroxene and olivine; cement is made from calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide, and talcum powder from the mineral talc
Snapshots summary: minerals are natural, solid substances with a fixed chemical composition, most often compounds but rarely pure elements

concepts.name: Mixtures: components, uniform and non-uniform types
concepts.description: Mixtures form when two or more substances are combined without a chemical reaction, each keeping its own properties; they are classed as uniform or non-uniform depending on whether their components can be told apart.
concepts.idea: A mixture is two or more substances combined so that each keeps its own properties and none react chemically; if the components can be seen separately it is non-uniform, and if they cannot be told apart even under a microscope it is uniform.
concepts.rule: When two or more substances are mixed, where each substance retains its properties, it is called a mixture. The individual substances that make up a mixture are called its components, and the components of a mixture do not react chemically with each other. In some mixtures the components, like green gram, chickpeas, onion and tomato in a sprout salad, are easy to see; such mixtures, where the different components are generally visible with the naked eye or with a magnifying device, are non-uniform in nature. In other mixtures, such as sugar dissolved in water, the components cannot be seen separately even with the help of a microscope; such mixtures, where the components are evenly distributed and cannot be distinguished, are uniform in nature. Air is a uniform mixture of mainly nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour; oxygen is needed by most living beings and helps combustion, while nitrogen, about 78 percent of air, does not take part in combustion. Lime water (a solution of calcium hydroxide) turns milky when carbon dioxide from the air reacts with it to form calcium carbonate and water, which is used to confirm the presence of carbon dioxide in air, and a black sheet of paper left near an open window collects tiny dust particles, showing that dust is suspended in air as a pollutant rather than being part of the air itself. Some mixtures of metals, called alloys, are uniform even though several metals are combined: stainless steel is a uniform mixture of iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon, mixed so thoroughly that no single metal can be seen separately, while brass (copper and zinc) and bronze (copper and tin) are other examples of alloys.
concepts.example: Sugar dissolved in water is a uniform mixture, while a sprout salad of green gram, chickpeas, onion and tomato is a non-uniform mixture.

concepts.name: Pure substances: the scientific meaning of 'pure'
concepts.description: The word 'pure' means something different in science than in everyday life: a scientifically pure substance has no other substance present in it and consists of only one type of particle.
concepts.idea: In common usage 'pure' means unadulterated, but in science a pure substance is one with no other substance present in it, made of only one type of particle, that cannot be split into other kinds of matter by a physical process.
concepts.rule: The word 'pure' has slightly different meanings in common usage and in science. In common usage, 'pure' means unadulterated products. Adulteration is an illegal process of adding substances which are cheaper, or of a poorer quality, to a product, usually done to increase the quantity or reduce the manufacturing cost; this deteriorates the quality of the product and can also make it hazardous to health. In science, however, a pure substance is the one that has no other substance present in it; a pure substance is a kind of matter that cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by any physical process, and when a scientist says something is pure, it means the substance consists of the same type of particles throughout. For a scientist, even products that look pure on their packaging, such as milk, ghee and spices, can be considered impure if they are actually made of more than one substance.
concepts.example: A packet labelled 'pure' spices might still be impure in the scientific sense if it is made of more than one type of particle.

concepts.name: Elements: atoms and molecules
concepts.description: Elements are pure substances made of identical atoms that cannot be broken down further, shown by passing electric current through water to obtain hydrogen and oxygen gas.
concepts.idea: An element is a pure substance made up of identical particles called atoms, which cannot be broken down into simpler substances; atoms of most elements combine to form molecules.
concepts.rule: Passing electric current through acidified water produces gas at each terminal of the battery; a pop sound when a burning candle is brought near one test tube identifies hydrogen gas, and the flame glowing brighter near the other test tube identifies oxygen gas, showing that water is composed of two different constituents, hydrogen and oxygen (Water gives Hydrogen + Oxygen). Hydrogen and oxygen are pure substances and are termed elements. Each element is made up of identical particles called atoms, which are different from the particles of any other element. Elements are substances that cannot be further broken down into simpler substances; they are the building blocks of all matter. Some other examples of elements are gold, silver, sulfur and carbon. The atoms of most elements cannot exist independently; two or more such atoms combine and form a stable particle of that element called a molecule. For example, two atoms of hydrogen combine to form one molecule of hydrogen, and two atoms of oxygen combine to form one molecule of oxygen.
concepts.example: Passing electric current through acidified water splits it into hydrogen gas (identified by a pop sound) and oxygen gas (identified by a brighter flame), showing water is made of these two elements.

concepts.name: Compounds: fixed-ratio combination of elements
concepts.description: Compounds are entirely new substances formed when different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio, shown by decomposing sugar on heating and by heating iron with sulfur to form iron sulfide.
concepts.idea: A compound forms when different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio to make something entirely new, with different properties from its constituent elements, and its elements cannot be separated by physical means.
concepts.rule: In water, the particles of hydrogen and oxygen are so tightly attached to each other that it is generally impossible to separate them by physical methods; that is why water is a compound. Compounds are formed when different elements combine in fixed ratios to form something entirely new, and the properties of a compound are different from those of the elements forming it; the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen atoms in water is 2:1. Sodium, a soft metal, and chlorine, a hazardous gas, combine to form sodium chloride (common salt), made up of particles of sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio. Heating sugar in a boiling tube makes it turn brown and then char to leave behind carbon (charcoal), with water droplets forming inside the tube from the sugar itself; since water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, sugar must be a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, not an element. In Activity 8.5, Sample A, an unheated mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder, still shows visible black and yellow particles, is attracted by a magnet, and reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give iron chloride and a colourless, odourless gas (hydrogen) that pops with a flame. Sample B, formed by heating Sample A and grinding the resulting black mass, is the compound iron sulfide: it has a uniform colour and texture throughout, is not attracted by a magnet, and reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give iron chloride and hydrogen sulfide gas, which has a rotten-egg odour; iron and sulfur can no longer be separated in this compound.
concepts.example: Heating iron filings and sulfur powder together forms the compound iron sulfide, which, unlike the original mixture, is not attracted by a magnet.

concepts.name: Using elements, compounds and mixtures in daily life
concepts.description: Elements, compounds and mixtures each have their own uses in daily life and technology, from breathing air and drinking water to building bridges, making medicines, and designing stronger materials like alloys.
concepts.idea: Elements like iron and aluminium are used directly for their own properties, compounds are designed by chemists for uses such as medicines and fertilisers, and mixtures are engineered, as in alloys and building materials, for properties the pure substances alone do not have.
concepts.rule: Elements, compounds and mixtures are all around us. The air we breathe is a mixture of gases like oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide. Water, which is essential for life, is a compound made of the elements hydrogen and oxygen. Elements like iron and aluminium are used to construct bridges, buildings and vehicles. Understanding these concepts is the key to innovation: chemists study how elements combine to create compounds, enabling them to invent life-saving medicines and vaccines to fight diseases, and this knowledge also helps in creating fertilisers that enhance crop production to feed the growing human population. Engineers and material scientists rely on their understanding of compounds and mixtures to design materials with unique properties; for example, they have developed alloys like stainless steel, which is stronger and more durable than pure iron. Wood, steel and concrete, used as building materials, are all mixtures.
concepts.example: Stainless steel, an alloy of iron, nickel, chromium and carbon, is used instead of pure iron because it is stronger and more durable.

concepts.name: Minerals: native elements and compound minerals
concepts.description: Most rocks are mixtures of minerals; a few minerals, called native minerals, are pure elements, while most minerals are compounds made of more than one element.
concepts.idea: Most rocks are a mixture of minerals; native minerals are pure elements such as gold or sulfur, while most minerals are compounds such as quartz or calcite, and many everyday products are made from minerals.
concepts.rule: Most rocks are a mixture of minerals, which can be viewed with the eyes, or by using a magnifying glass or a microscope. Some of the minerals are called native minerals, which are pure elements and not compounds; these can be metals, such as gold, silver and copper, or non-metals like sulfur and carbon. Most of the minerals are compounds made up of more than one element; some common examples of minerals include quartz, calcite, mica, pyroxene and olivine. Many things used in everyday life are made up of minerals or elements extracted from minerals: cement is made from calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide, which are minerals or are obtained from minerals, and talcum powder is made from the mineral talc. Minerals are natural, solid substances found on Earth, with a fixed chemical composition; most often they are compounds, but rarely they can also be pure elements.
concepts.example: Gold is a native mineral that is a pure element, while quartz is a mineral that is a compound.
